question.text: A fund reports a Geometric Mean Return (GMR) of 11.5% and an Arithmetic Mean Return (AMR) of 12.8%. Which of the following statements is MOST accurate regarding this relationship?

answer.text: The data is erroneous because GMR should always be higher than AMR
The GMR is higher because it accounts for compounding effects
This is expected because GMR is always less than or equal to AMR, and the two are equal only when all periodic returns are identical
GMR equals AMR when returns are volatile; they differ only when returns are constant

explanation.text: The Logic: Per NISM Series X-A pages 271-272, AMR is the arithmetic average of periodic returns and GMR is the compound (geometric) return. Page 272 states that the geometric average return is always less than the arithmetic average return, except when all yearly returns are identical. Here 11.5% < 12.8% is fully consistent with that rule. The Trap: Saying GMR > AMR reverses the fundamental inequality from page 272. Saying GMR accounts for compounding is true but compounding with varying returns reduces, not raises, the geometric average. The last option reverses the equality condition. Note: GMR and AMR are equal only when every yearly return is the same; any variation across periods pushes GMR below AMR.
